triage.name: Cough
triage.reason: Extremely common presenting symptom with a broad differential that students must narrow by history, exam and targeted testing.

demographics: Cough is among the most common symptoms prompting outpatient visits in all age groups.
Viral upper respiratory infections are more frequent in young children.

chief_complaints.text: I can't stop coughing at night

hpi.onset: Variable; often starts during or shortly after a cold or upper respiratory symptoms
hpi.duration: Acute cough lasts less than 3 weeks; subacute 3–8 weeks; chronic more than 8 weeks
hpi.progression: May begin dry and later become productive; can be intermittent or paroxysmal, especially at night
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; occasionally severe enough to disturb sleep or cause vomiting
hpi.timing: Often worse at night, on first awakening, or after exposure to triggers

atypical.how_it_differs: Young children may have post-tussive vomiting, a barking cough with croup, or apnea with pertussis; they often cannot describe sputum or chest discomfort.
May present with cough from medications, GERD, or heart failure; fever and wheezing may be absent even with significant infection.
GERD and rhinitis of pregnancy commonly cause cough; dyspnea from normal pregnancy may confound assessment.
May have little or no fever with serious infections, and a broader differential includes opportunistic pathogens.

general.moderate: Mild discomfort, occasional coughing fits; speaks in full sentences
general.severe: Visible respiratory distress, sits upright, speaks in short sentences, using accessory muscles
general.critical: Exhausted, diaphoretic, cyanotic, lethargic, tripod position

findings.maneuver: Auscultate posterior chest during full inspiration

findings.finding: Coarse rhonchi that clear with coughing

findings.maneuver: Auscultate posterior chest while patient says 'E'
Examine jugular venous pressure at 45 degrees
Observe chest wall movement during breathing

labs.caveat: Peripheral eosinophilia can support an atopic or eosinophilic cause such as asthma, allergic rhinitis, or eosinophilic bronchitis, but many patients with these causes have a normal count.
Marked lymphocytosis is classic for pertussis, especially in young unvaccinated children; adults often have milder or no lymphocytosis.

imaging.preferred_when: First-line imaging for chronic cough or suspected pneumonia
Abnormal chest x-ray, suspected pulmonary embolism, interstitial lung disease, or malignancy in high-risk patients

initial.why: Evaluate for pneumonia, heart failure, mass, or chronic lung disease
initial.only_if: pneumonia is suspected (fever, tachypnea, focal crackles, egophony) OR cough has lasted >8 weeks

initial.why: Rule out pregnancy before CT chest or other ionizing radiation
initial.only_if: CT chest is being considered and the patient could be pregnant

initial.why: Detect influenza in patients with acute cough and fever during influenza season
initial.only_if: influenza is circulating and symptoms are compatible

initial.why: Detect SARS-CoV-2 when acute cough is accompanied by fever, myalgia, or known exposure
initial.only_if: COVID-19 is circulating or the patient has a concerning exposure

confirmatory.why: Confirm Bordetella pertussis in the right clinical setting
confirmatory.only_if: cough ≥2 weeks with paroxysms, post-tussive vomiting, whoop, or known exposure

supporting.why: Leukocytosis can support bacterial infection when pneumonia or sepsis is possible
supporting.only_if: systemic symptoms or signs suggest bacterial infection

supporting.why: Diagnose asthma or COPD in chronic cough; assess airway obstruction
supporting.only_if: chronic cough (>8 weeks) or suspected asthma/COPD

supporting.why: Evaluate for pulmonary embolism, interstitial lung disease, bronchiectasis, or malignancy
supporting.only_if: abnormal chest x-ray, hemoptysis, significant smoking history, or suspected pulmonary embolism

not_indicated.why: Does not reliably distinguish viral from bacterial causes of cough in primary care
Not indicated unless there is a specific concern for pulmonary embolism (e.g., pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, risk factors)
Not needed unless heart failure is suspected based on history and exam
Not needed unless the patient is in respiratory distress or hypoxemia is present

decision_points: Do not order chest x-ray for most acute coughs with a normal exam and no red flags
Test for pertussis only when the cough has typical paroxysms or post-tussive vomiting
Obtain pregnancy test before CT chest in anyone who could be pregnant
Consider spirometry early in chronic cough to evaluate for asthma or COPD

differential.name: Acute bronchitis
differential.why_considered: Acute cough often follows a viral upper respiratory infection and is the most common cause of acute cough in otherwise healthy adults.

history: Cough starts dry and later becomes productive
Preceded by sore throat, rhinorrhea, and malaise
No chronic lung disease or smoking-related symptoms

differential.name: Upper airway cough syndrome
differential.why_considered: Chronic cough may be caused by postnasal drip from allergic or nonallergic rhinitis, sinusitis, or rhinitis medicamentosa.

history: Sensation of mucus dripping into the throat
Frequent throat clearing
Nasal congestion or rhinorrhea
Worse when lying down
exam: Cobblestone appearance of the posterior oropharynx
labs: Peripheral eosinophilia may be present with allergic rhinitis
imaging: Sinus films may show mucosal thickening

differential.name: Asthma
differential.why_considered: Chronic cough, especially at night or with triggers, may be the only manifestation of cough-variant asthma.

history: Episodic cough worse at night or early morning
Triggered by cold air, exercise, allergens, or strong smells
Personal or family history of atopy
imaging: May show hyperinflation during an exacerbation

differential.name: Gastroesophageal reflux disease
differential.why_considered: Reflux is a common cause of chronic cough, especially when nocturnal or after meals.

history: Cough worse after meals or when lying flat
Heartburn, sour taste, or regurgitation
Hoarseness or throat clearing
exam: May have dental erosions or posterior pharyngeal erythema
imaging: Barium swallow may show reflux but is not diagnostic

differential.name: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
differential.why_considered: Chronic productive cough in a smoker or ex-smoker suggests COPD.

history: Chronic cough with sputum for months to years
Progressive exertional dyspnea
Heavy tobacco smoking history
exam: Barrel chest and use of accessory muscles in advanced disease
labs: No eosinophilia unless there is coexisting asthma
imaging: Chest x-ray may show hyperinflation, flattened diaphragms, and increased retrosternal airspace

differential.name: Community-acquired pneumonia
differential.why_considered: Acute cough with fever, sputum, and systemic symptoms may indicate pneumonia.
differential.trigger: Fever, tachypnea, and focal crackles on lung exam

history: Acute cough productive of purulent sputum
Fever, chills, and pleuritic chest pain
Dyspnea
exam: Focal crackles, bronchial breath sounds, or egophony
imaging: Chest x-ray with focal airspace consolidation

differential.name: Pertussis
differential.why_considered: Paroxysmal cough with post-tussive vomiting or whoop, especially in children or unvaccinated adults.
differential.trigger: Post-tussive vomiting, whoop, or cough lasting more than 2 weeks with known exposure

history: Cough in paroxysms, often with an inspiratory whoop
Post-tussive vomiting
Cough lasting more than 2 weeks despite usual treatment
Exposure to a confirmed case
exam: May have conjunctival hemorrhages from coughing
labs: Marked lymphocytosis, especially in young children
Pertussis PCR positive from nasopharyngeal swab

differential.name: Heart failure
differential.why_considered: Chronic cough, especially nocturnal or with exertion, may be due to pulmonary congestion.
differential.trigger: Orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, or bilateral leg swelling

history: Dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
Bilateral leg swelling
Known hypertension, coronary disease, or cardiomyopathy
imaging: Chest x-ray with cardiomegaly, pulmonary vascular congestion, or pleural effusions

differential.name: Pulmonary embolism
differential.why_considered: Acute cough with pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, or risk factors may be due to pulmonary embolism.
differential.trigger: Pleuritic chest pain, unexplained dyspnea, or risk factors for venous thromboembolism

history: Sudden pleuritic chest pain
Dyspnea at rest or with minimal exertion
Risk factors: recent surgery, immobilization, cancer, oral contraceptives
exam: Unilateral leg swelling if DVT present
labs: ABG may show hypoxemia with respiratory alkalosis
imaging: CT pulmonary angiography shows filling defect
Ventilation-perfusion scan may be used if CT contraindicated

differential.name: Lung cancer
differential.why_considered: Chronic cough, especially with hemoptysis, weight loss, or smoking history, must prompt evaluation for malignancy.
differential.trigger: Hemoptysis, significant weight loss, or a long smoking history with changing cough

history: Cough that has changed in character or persists for weeks
Hemoptysis
Unintentional weight loss
Heavy smoking history
exam: Focal decreased breath sounds or wheeze if tumor obstructs an airway
labs: Anemia or elevated alkaline phosphatase if metastatic
imaging: Chest x-ray with nodule, mass, or hilar prominence
CT chest shows suspicious lesion; PET-CT and biopsy for diagnosis

severity.mild: Acute cough with no respiratory distress, normal vital signs, and no concerning exam findings. Cough may be dry or mildly productive and does not interfere with sleep or daily activities.
severity.moderate: Coughing fits interrupt sleep or daily activities. Patient may have low-grade fever, mild tachypnea, or scattered wheezes/rhonchi. Oxygen saturation is normal.
severity.severe: Paroxysmal cough with post-tussive vomiting, syncope, or respiratory distress. Patient may have hypoxemia, focal crackles, wheezes, or signs of pneumonia or pulmonary embolism. Requires urgent evaluation and likely imaging.

red_flags.meaning: Possible lung cancer, tuberculosis, bronchiectasis, or pulmonary embolism
Possible pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, heart failure, or upper airway obstruction
Upper airway obstruction, such as foreign body, croup, or anaphylaxis
Respiratory failure; needs immediate oxygen and evaluation
Possible pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, or pneumothorax
Severe cough causing cough syncope; rule out underlying cardiac or pulmonary disease

complications.name: Cough syncope
clues: Loss of consciousness during a coughing paroxysm
Rapid recovery after the cough stops

complications.name: Rib fracture
clues: Localized chest wall pain worse with coughing or deep breathing

complications.name: Urinary incontinence
clues: More common in women with prior childbirth

complications.name: Subconjunctival hemorrhage
clues: Painless red patch on the white of the eye after forceful coughing

complications.name: Pneumothorax
clues: Sudden pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea during a coughing fit
May occur in patients with underlying bullous lung disease

special_populations.differences: Young children may have cough with post-tussive vomiting due to pertussis; foreign body aspiration should be considered with sudden onset; croup causes barking cough and stridor. Avoid over-the-counter cough and cold medicines under age 4.
More likely to have medication-induced cough (ACE inhibitors), heart failure, COPD, or lung cancer. Fever and wheezing may be absent even with significant infection. Coughing can cause rib fractures.

GERD and rhinitis of pregnancy commonly cause cough. Avoid unnecessary ionizing radiation; use ultrasound or MRI if imaging is needed. Pertussis vaccination is recommended during each pregnancy to protect the newborn.

May have little or no fever with serious infections. Broader differential includes tuberculosis, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, fungal infections, and cytomegalovirus. Evaluate more aggressively and obtain chest imaging early.

key_questions.question: When did the cough start and how long has it been present?
key_questions.looking_for: Duration: acute (<3 weeks), subacute (3-8 weeks), or chronic (>8 weeks)

key_questions.question: Is the cough dry or productive? If productive, what does the sputum look like?
key_questions.looking_for: Dry vs productive sputum; purulent sputum may suggest bacterial infection

key_questions.question: Have you coughed up any blood?
key_questions.looking_for: Hemoptysis (frank blood or blood-streaked sputum) concerning for malignancy, TB, PE

key_questions.question: Do you have shortness of breath, chest pain, or wheezing?
key_questions.looking_for: Dyspnea or pleuritic chest pain suggests pneumonia, PE, heart failure; wheezing suggests asthma/COPD

key_questions.question: Have you had fevers, chills, or night sweats?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever suggests infection; night sweats may indicate TB or lymphoma

key_questions.question: Do you have heartburn, a sour taste in your mouth, or worsening when lying flat?
key_questions.looking_for: Reflux as a cause of chronic cough

key_questions.question: Do you have nasal congestion, postnasal drip, or frequent throat clearing?
key_questions.looking_for: Upper airway cough syndrome from allergic or nonallergic rhinitis

key_questions.question: Have you had any post-tussive vomiting or known exposure to pertussis?
key_questions.looking_for: Paroxysmal cough with post-tussive vomiting or whoop suggests pertussis

key_questions.question: What medications do you take? Have you recently started an ACE inhibitor?
key_questions.looking_for: ACE inhibitor-induced cough; discontinuing the drug should resolve cough within weeks

key_questions.question: Do you smoke or vape? Any secondhand smoke or occupational exposures?
key_questions.looking_for: Tobacco smoke is a key risk factor for chronic bronchitis, COPD, lung cancer; occupational irritants

key_questions.question: Do you have a history of asthma, COPD, heart failure, or allergic rhinitis?
key_questions.looking_for: Underlying conditions that commonly cause chronic cough

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy influences diagnosis and imaging safety; GERD and rhinitis of pregnancy common

key_questions.question: Have you been around anyone with a cough or known pertussis?

reasoning_points: Duration classifies cough as acute, subacute, or chronic and directs the differential
Character of cough, sputum quality, and associated symptoms narrow the likely cause
Medication history screens for ACE inhibitor use as a reversible cause
Social history includes tobacco, occupational exposures, and sick contacts
Respiratory exam looks for crackles, wheezes, rhonchi, or consolidation
Red flags such as hemoptysis, dyspnea, weight loss, and cyanosis are excluded
Targeted tests include chest x-ray for pneumonia or chronic cough, spirometry for asthma or COPD, and pertussis PCR for paroxysmal cough
Most acute coughs are viral and self-limited; antibiotics are not routinely indicated
Chronic cough is most often due to upper airway cough syndrome, asthma, GERD, or COPD
Life-threatening causes such as pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, heart failure, and lung cancer are considered and ruled out

easy: Young adult or child with acute cough after a viral upper respiratory infection
Normal vital signs and clear lungs or only mild rhonchi
No chronic symptoms or red flags
Clinically consistent with acute bronchitis or viral URI
medium: Middle-aged adult with chronic cough at night or after meals suggesting GERD or asthma
Cough-variant asthma with normal chest exam and episodic nocturnal cough
ACE inhibitor-induced dry cough in a hypertensive patient
Upper airway cough syndrome with postnasal drip and throat clearing
hard: Older adult smoker with cough, weight loss, and hemoptysis suggesting lung cancer
Post-tussive vomiting and paroxysmal cough in an under-vaccinated adult or child (pertussis)
Cough with pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea in a patient with risk factors for pulmonary embolism
Chronic cough in a patient with heart failure presenting only with nocturnal cough and orthopnea
Immunocompromised patient with minimal symptoms but serious opportunistic infection
